title: How rogue officers turned a nationwide camera network into a tool for stalking

reading.body:
This incident shows a failure of access control and oversight in a deployed surveillance system. A license plate reader network intended for law enforcement was queried by an authorized user for a personal purpose, tracking an estranged spouse. The system was used outside the conditions it was built for, and no automated or human check stopped the misuse before it became a stalking case.

Catching this would have required audit logging of every query, review of unusual patterns such as repeated lookups of a person not under investigation, and a process to flag or block queries that do not match an active case. The charges are allegations, not findings, and the reports do not establish departmental knowledge or intent.

reports.title: Kechi police lieutenant arrested for using police technology to stalk wife
Former Kechi police lieutenant convicted on stalking charges
A former police officer has been sentenced in Sedgwick County District Court
‘You were spotted’: KS officer who used police cameras to stalk estranged wife sentenced
Wichita moves to tighten access, increase oversight on secretive police surveillance program
How rogue officers turned a nationwide camera network into a tool for stalking

summary:
Victor Heiar, a lieutenant with the Kechi Police Department, was arrested by Wichita Police after unlawfully using the department's license plate reader technology to track his estranged wife's location. Heiar has been charged with one count of stalking and one count of unlawful acts concerning computers, and has been removed from his position. He is currently held in Sedgwick County Jail.

A defense attorney noted that misusing access to confidential law enforcement information for personal purposes becomes a criminal matter when repeated and abusive enough to constitute stalking. A private investigator commented that while the situation requires investigation, he considers such incidents isolated and not indicative of common problems within police departments. The Wichita and Sedgwick County law enforcement agencies recently received 1.6 million dollars in federal funding for license plate readers and camera technology.
